Heritage walk in Orchha: Bundela palaces, temples and chhatris

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

A heritage walk in Orchha covers the 16th and 17th century capital of the Bundela Rajputs on the Betwa river: the fort island with Raja Mahal and Jahangir Mahal, the tall Chaturbhuj Temple, the Ram Raja Temple, Lakshminarayan Temple with its murals, and the riverside chhatris. Almost everything is within a 2 km walk.

We arrange Orchha heritage walks on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, led by an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi.

Why Orchha matters

Orchha is a small town today, but from 1531 to the late 18th century it was the capital of the Bundela kingdom in Bundelkhand. Its rulers allied with and sometimes fought the Mughals, and their buildings show a mix of Rajput and Mughal ideas: domes and chhatris, palace courtyards, painted interiors and temples raised on tall platforms.

Because the capital moved to Tikamgarh in 1783, Orchha was not rebuilt by later rulers. Its palaces, temples, gardens and cenotaphs survive close together, which makes it one of the easiest places in India to see a complete 16th and 17th century royal town on foot.

Layers of Orchha's history

Rudra Pratap Singh founded Orchha in 1531 on a bend of the Betwa. His successor Madhukar Shah built much of the Raja Mahal and, according to local tradition, brought an image of Rama from Ayodhya; the palace where it was placed became the Ram Raja Temple, unusual because Rama is worshipped there as a king.

Bir Singh Deo (ruled 1605 to 1627) was close to Jahangir, whom he had helped before his accession, and built the Jahangir Mahal to receive him, along with the Chaturbhuj Temple's later stages and the Phool Bagh garden. He also built the Bir Singh Palace at Datia nearby. Later rulers added the Lakshminarayan Temple (1622, with 19th century murals) and the chhatris on the river, the cenotaphs of the Bundela kings.

Shah Jahan's armies took Orchha in the 1630s for a time, and Bundela power later shifted to Panna under Chhatrasal. The Mughal architecture and forts of India guides help place Orchha in its wider world.

Places a heritage walk in Orchha covers

  1. Raja Mahal 16th to 17th century

    Main palace of the Bundela kings with painted ceilings and walls.

  2. Jahangir Mahal early 17th century

    Bir Singh Deo's palace built to host Jahangir, with domes, balconies and a courtyard.

  3. Rai Praveen Mahal late 16th to 17th century

    Smaller palace and garden linked to the court poet and musician Rai Praveen.

  4. Sheesh Mahal, Orchha 18th century

    Later palace building on the fort complex, now a hotel.

  5. Ram Raja Temple 16th century

    Palace turned temple, where Rama is worshipped as king.

  6. Chaturbhuj Temple late 16th to early 17th century

    Tall temple on a high plinth with spires, a cross-shaped plan and steep stairs.

  7. Phool Bagh 17th century

    Palace garden with a summer pavilion and water channels.

  8. Lakshminarayan Temple 1622, murals 19th century

    Fort-like temple on a hill with murals of myths, battles and the 1857 era.

  9. Chhatris on the Betwa 17th to 18th century

    Cenotaphs of the Bundela rulers in a row along the river.

  10. Saawan Bhadon pillars 17th century

    Pair of towers near Phool Bagh, thought to have helped cool the palace.

  11. Betwa river and bridge landscape

    Viewpoint over the chhatris and the fort island.

Walking routes in Orchha

The fort island

About 2 to 3 hours

Raja Mahal → Jahangir Mahal → Rai Praveen Mahal → Sheesh Mahal, Orchha

Temples and garden

About 2 hours

Ram Raja Temple → Chaturbhuj Temple → Phool Bagh → Saawan Bhadon pillars → Lakshminarayan Temple

The river at sunset

About 1 to 2 hours

Chhatris on the Betwa → Betwa river and bridge

Museums in Orchha

  • Jahangir Mahal galleries. Small ASI and state displays inside the palace on Bundela history and finds.
  • Government Museum, Jhansi. Regional museum in Jhansi with sculpture and Bundelkhand history, a short drive away.

Best time for a walk

October to March. The light on the chhatris is best in the late afternoon.

What you see on a walk

In the Jahangir Mahal, students read a square palace plan built around a courtyard, with corner towers, domes, hanging balconies and blue tile traces. In Raja Mahal, painted ceilings and walls show Ramayana and Bhagavata scenes and courtly life. The Chaturbhuj Temple, on a high plinth, mixes a temple plan with palace-like scale and Mughal-style domes and arches.

At the chhatris, look at how memorials for kings borrow the temple's tower shape. A lecture such as Reading a temple or Temple superstructures gives students the vocabulary, and Heritage photography suits the riverside.

Orchha for school and college groups

Orchha is offered within Stupas, caves and temples of central India or as a study tour built for your group, usually with Gwalior and Khajuraho.

Orchha is about 16 km from Jhansi, which has a railway junction and the Jhansi Fort of Rani Lakshmibai. The town itself is compact and walkable. The fort island, temples and chhatris are within easy reach, and stairs in the palaces are steep and dark in places, so keep groups small inside. The Ram Raja Temple is an active temple; check timings and dress rules.

Questions people ask

What are the main historical places in Orchha?

Raja Mahal and Jahangir Mahal on the fort island, Rai Praveen Mahal, the Ram Raja Temple, Chaturbhuj Temple, Lakshminarayan Temple, Phool Bagh and the chhatris on the Betwa.

Who built Orchha?

The Bundela Rajputs. Rudra Pratap Singh founded the town in 1531, and Madhukar Shah and Bir Singh Deo built most of the palaces and temples in the late 16th and early 17th centuries.

Is Orchha good for a school heritage walk?

Yes. It is compact, quiet and walkable, with palaces, temples and memorials close together. Keep groups small on the dark palace stairs and visit the chhatris late in the day.

Are there museums in Orchha?

There are small displays inside Jahangir Mahal. For a fuller collection, add the Government Museum in Jhansi, about 16 km away, with Jhansi Fort.

Can Talaash Heritage arrange an Orchha visit?

Yes, on request for schools, colleges, companies and private groups, with an archaeologist or historian, in English or Hindi, often with Gwalior and Khajuraho.
